solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', ionisation constant of water and its ionic product
solution.final_answer: Option B: 5.0 × 10⁻¹² mol L⁻¹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For the gaseous equilibrium 4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) ⇌ 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(g), the equilibrium constant expression K_c is:

solution.explanation: K_c is the product of the equilibrium concentrations of the products, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, divided by the corresponding product for the reactants. Water here is a gas, so it appears in the expression.
solution.why_others_wrong: The first option is the expression for the reverse reaction (1/K_c). The second ignores the coefficients. The fourth leaves out H₂O(g), which may be omitted only when water is a pure liquid.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', law of chemical equilibrium and equilibrium constant
solution.final_answer: Option C: [NO]⁴[H₂O]⁶ / ([NH₃]⁴[O₂]⁵)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: At 298 K, a solution of pH 3 has a lower H₃O⁺ concentration than a solution of pH 5.
Statement II: At 298 K, a solution of pH 9 is acidic.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: pH = −log[H₃O⁺]. A lower pH means a higher [H₃O⁺]: pH 3 has [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻³ M, which is 100 times that of pH 5 (10⁻⁵ M). So Statement I is false. At 298 K, pH > 7 is basic, so a solution of pH 9 is basic, not acidic: Statement II is false.
steps: pH 3 → 10⁻³ M; pH 5 → 10⁻⁵ M → pH 3 is 100 times more acidic (I false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', the pH scale
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (term) with List-II (meaning).

List-I:
A. Common ion effect
B. Buffer solution
C. Hydrolysis of a salt
D. Solubility product

List-II:
I. Product of the molar concentrations of the ions in a saturated solution, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient
II. Reaction of the cation and/or anion of a salt with water that changes the pH
III. Suppression of the ionisation of a weak electrolyte by adding a strong electrolyte having an ion in common with it
IV. Solution that resists a change in pH when a small amount of acid or base is added

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Each term is defined in the study of ionic equilibria in solution.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange the common ion effect with buffer action, or hydrolysis with the solubility product.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', common ion effect, hydrolysis of salts, buffer solutions, solubility product
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a homogeneous equilibrium?

solution.explanation: In a homogeneous equilibrium all the reactants and products are in the same phase. In N₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2NO all species are gases.
steps: N₂(g), O₂(g), NO(g): one phase → homogeneous
The other three involve a solid or a liquid together with a gas → heterogeneous
solution.why_others_wrong: CaCO₃/CaO with CO₂, liquid water with its vapour, and carbon with steam each contain more than one phase.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', homogeneous and heterogeneous equilibria
solution.final_answer: Option A: N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: At a certain temperature: N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), K₁ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ and 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), K₂ = 2.5 × 10⁵. The equilibrium constant of N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) at the same temperature is:

solution.concept: Equilibrium constant of a reaction obtained by adding two reactions
solution.explanation: When two equations are added, the equilibrium constant of the overall reaction is the product of their equilibrium constants (the concentration of the common species NO cancels).
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.5 × 10⁵ adds the two constants. 6.25 × 10⁸ and 1.6 × 10⁻⁹ divide one by the other, as if one equation were reversed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', equilibrium constant for combined reactions
solution.final_answer: Option B: 100

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), K_c = 50 at a certain temperature. A mixture at this temperature has [H₂] = 0.10 M, [I₂] = 0.20 M and [HI] = 0.50 M. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: Q_c = 12.5; the net reaction proceeds in the backward direction
Q_c = 25; the net reaction proceeds in the forward direction
Q_c = 0.08; the net reaction proceeds in the forward direction
Q_c = 12.5; the net reaction proceeds in the forward direction

solution.concept: Reaction quotient and the direction of reaction
solution.explanation: Q_c has the same form as K_c but uses the actual concentrations. If Q_c < K_c, the reaction moves forward (towards products) to reach equilibrium; if Q_c > K_c, it moves backward.
solution.why_others_wrong: With Q_c < K_c the reaction cannot go backward. 25 forgets to square [HI]. 0.08 is the reciprocal of Q_c (the expression is inverted).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', predicting the direction of the reaction
solution.final_answer: Option D: Q_c = 12.5; the net reaction proceeds in the forward direction

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: When solid NH₄Cl is dissolved in an aqueous solution of NH₄OH (ammonia solution), the pH of the solution:

solution.concept: Common ion effect on a weak base
solution.explanation: NH₄OH ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. NH₄Cl is a strong electrolyte and supplies the common ion NH₄⁺, which shifts this equilibrium to the left. [OH⁻] decreases, so the pH falls (the solution becomes a basic buffer).
steps: Extra NH₄⁺ suppresses ionisation of NH₄OH → [OH⁻] falls → pH decreases
solution.why_others_wrong: The pH cannot rise because [OH⁻] falls. It does change, and the mixture remains basic (a basic buffer), so it does not become 7.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', common ion effect in the ionisation of acids and bases
solution.final_answer: Option C: Decreases

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Pure water at 350 K is neutral even though its pH is less than 7.
Reason (R): The ionic product of water, K_w, decreases with rise in temperature.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Neutrality and the effect of temperature on K_w
solution.explanation: Ionisation of water is endothermic, so K_w increases with temperature; at 350 K, [H₃O⁺] = √K_w is greater than 10⁻⁷ M and the pH is below 7. Pure water is still neutral because [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻]. A is true; R is false (K_w increases, not decreases, with temperature).
steps: Pure water: [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] at every temperature → neutral
K_w rises with T → [H₃O⁺] > 10⁻⁷ M → pH < 7 (A true)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', ionisation constant of water
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at equilibrium in a closed vessel, adding more H₂ at constant volume and temperature decreases the amount of HI at the new equilibrium.
Statement II: Adding more H₂ at constant temperature increases the value of K_c for this reaction.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Le Chatelier's principle: effect of concentration
solution.explanation: Adding a reactant makes Q_c < K_c, so the equilibrium shifts forward and more HI forms: Statement I is false. K_c depends only on temperature, so it is unchanged: Statement II is false.
steps: Extra H₂ → Q_c < K_c → shift forward → more HI (I false)
K_c changes only with temperature (II false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', factors affecting equilibria: effect of concentration change
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (gaseous equilibrium) with List-II (unit of K_p, with pressures in bar).

List-I:
A. N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)
B. N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
C. H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
D. 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g)

List-II:
I. bar⁻¹
II. No unit
III. bar⁻²
IV. bar

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The unit of K_p is bar^Δn, where Δn = (moles of gaseous products) − (moles of gaseous reactants).
steps: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI: Δn = 0 → no unit → II
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes reverse the sign of Δn for the NO₂–N₂O₄ pair, or mix up Δn = 0 and Δn = −2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', relationship between K_p and K_c; units of equilibrium constant
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
For the equilibrium PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), ΔH > 0, set up in a closed vessel, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Raising the temperature increases the equilibrium constant.
(b) Compressing the mixture to a smaller volume at constant temperature increases the amount of PCl₅.
(c) Adding a catalyst increases the amount of PCl₃ present at equilibrium.
(d) Removing some Cl₂ at constant volume shifts the equilibrium in the forward direction.
(e) K_p = K_c for this equilibrium.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: For an endothermic forward reaction, K increases with temperature. Compression favours the side with fewer moles of gas (1 mol PCl₅ against 2 mol of products). A catalyst speeds up both directions equally and does not change the equilibrium composition. Removing a product shifts the equilibrium forward. Here Δn = +1, so K_p = K_c(RT).
steps: (b) True: fewer gas moles on the left
(c) False: a catalyst does not shift equilibrium
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) or (e) are wrong; (a), (b) and (d) are all true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', factors affecting equilibria
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Equal volumes of 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M BaCl₂ and 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M Na₂SO₄ solutions are mixed at 298 K. K_sp(BaSO₄) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: Ionic product = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸; BaSO₄ does not precipitate

solution.concept: Predicting precipitation from the ionic product
solution.explanation: On mixing equal volumes, each concentration is halved. A precipitate forms when the ionic product [Ba²⁺][SO₄²⁻] exceeds K_sp.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.0 × 10⁻⁸ ignores the dilution on mixing, and 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ dilutes only one solution. An ionic product larger than K_sp means the solution is supersaturated, so precipitation does occur.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', solubility product: predicting precipitation
solution.final_answer: Option C: Ionic product = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸; BaSO₄ precipitates

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: CO₂ gas at an initial pressure of 0.50 atm is placed with excess solid carbon in a closed vessel and heated to a fixed temperature: CO₂(g) + C(s) ⇌ 2CO(g). At equilibrium the total pressure is 0.80 atm. K_p at this temperature is:

solution.explanation: The pure solid carbon does not appear in K_p. If CO₂ falls by x atm, CO rises by 2x atm, so the total pressure rises by x.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.0 atm forgets to square p(CO). 1.2 atm divides by the CO₂ consumed (0.30) instead of the CO₂ left (0.20). 0.45 atm uses x instead of 2x for p(CO).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', heterogeneous equilibria
solution.final_answer: Option D: 1.8 atm

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The degree of ionisation of pure water at 298 K is (K_w = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴; density of water = 1.0 g mL⁻¹; H = 1, O = 16):

solution.explanation: Degree of ionisation = (moles ionised per litre) / (total moles per litre). In pure water [H₃O⁺] = √K_w, and one litre of water (1000 g) contains 1000/18 = 55.6 mol.
steps: Molar concentration of water = 1000 / 18 = 55.6 mol L⁻¹
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ is [H₃O⁺] itself, not divided by the concentration of water. 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ divides K_w instead of √K_w. 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ is K_w.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', ionisation constant of water
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1.8 × 10⁻⁹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: At 298 K the solubility products are: AgCl 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, AgBr 5.0 × 10⁻¹³, AgI 8.3 × 10⁻¹⁷ and Ag₂CrO₄ 1.1 × 10⁻¹². Which salt has the highest molar solubility in pure water? (√1.8 = 1.34; ∛0.275 = 0.65)

solution.concept: Molar solubility from K_sp for salts of different formula types
solution.explanation: K_sp values can be compared directly only for salts of the same formula type. For AB, K_sp = s²; for A₂B, K_sp = (2s)²s = 4s³. Molar solubilities must be calculated before comparing.
solution.why_others_wrong: AgCl has the largest K_sp but a smaller molar solubility than Ag₂CrO₄, because K_sp of a 2 : 1 salt varies as s³. AgBr and AgI are much less soluble.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', solubility product constant
solution.final_answer: Option A: Ag₂CrO₄

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The pH of a buffer made of CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa changes greatly when the buffer is diluted ten times with water.
Reason (R): The pH of such a buffer depends on the ratio [CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH], as given by the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Effect of dilution on buffer pH
solution.explanation: pH = pK_a + log([CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH]). Dilution reduces both concentrations by the same factor, so the ratio and hence the pH stay practically unchanged. A is false; R is a true statement of the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.
steps: Dilution: ratio unchanged → pH almost unchanged (A false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', buffer solutions: designing a buffer
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The oxidation number of oxygen in dioxygen difluoride, O₂F₂, is:

solution.concept: Oxidation number rules: fluorine is always −1
solution.explanation: Fluorine, the most electronegative element, has oxidation number −1 in all its compounds. The sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule is zero.
solution.why_others_wrong: +2 is the value in OF₂, not O₂F₂. −1 is the value in peroxides, and −2 the usual value; neither applies when oxygen is bonded to fluorine.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Redox Reactions', oxidation number
solution.final_answer: Option C: +1

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In the dry (Leclanché) cell, the anode is:

options.text: The paste of manganese dioxide and carbon
The moist paste of ammonium chloride and zinc chloride

solution.explanation: The dry cell has a zinc container that also acts as the anode; the cathode is a carbon (graphite) rod surrounded by powdered MnO₂ and carbon. The space between is filled with a moist paste of NH₄Cl and ZnCl₂. At the anode Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻.
steps: Cathode: graphite rod in MnO₂ + carbon
solution.why_others_wrong: The graphite rod is the cathode, MnO₂ is reduced at the cathode, and the NH₄Cl–ZnCl₂ paste is the electrolyte.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', batteries: primary batteries
solution.final_answer: Option A: The zinc container

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In a galvanic cell, the electrode at which reduction takes place is called the cathode.
Statement II: In the conventional representation of a galvanic cell, the anode is written on the right-hand side.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation at the anode, so Statement I is true. By convention the anode (oxidation half-cell) is written on the left and the cathode on the right, e.g. Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s). Statement II is false.
steps: Anode on the left, cathode on the right (II false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', galvanic cells and their representation
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (quantity) with List-II (relation used to obtain it). (R = resistance, κ = conductivity, c = concentration, l = distance between electrodes, A = area of cross-section, G* = cell constant)

List-I:
A. Conductance (G)
B. Conductivity (κ)
C. Molar conductivity (Λm)
D. Cell constant (G*)

List-II:
I. κ / c
II. l / A
III. 1 / R
IV. G* / R

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance. Since R = ρ l/A, conductivity κ = 1/ρ = (l/A)(1/R) = G*/R. Molar conductivity is conductivity divided by concentration, and the cell constant is l/A.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange conductance with conductivity, or molar conductivity with the cell constant.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', conductance of electrolytic solutions
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For a strong electrolyte, Λm = Λ°m − A√c. Its molar conductivity is 120 S cm² mol⁻¹ at c = 0.04 mol L⁻¹ and 130 S cm² mol⁻¹ at c = 0.01 mol L⁻¹. Its limiting molar conductivity Λ°m is:

solution.explanation: Λm varies linearly with √c. Two data points fix the slope −A and the intercept Λ°m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 133.3 plots Λm against c instead of √c. 125 is the average of the two values. 130 takes the value at the lower concentration as the limiting value, without extrapolating to zero concentration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', variation of conductivity and molar conductivity with concentration
solution.final_answer: Option D: 140 S cm² mol⁻¹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In acidic medium, KMnO₄ oxidises iron(II) oxalate, FeC₂O₄, completely: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ and C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂, while MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺. The number of moles of KMnO₄ needed to oxidise 1 mol of FeC₂O₄ is:

solution.explanation: Moles of electrons lost by the reducing agent must equal moles of electrons gained by the oxidising agent. Both the Fe²⁺ and the oxalate ion in FeC₂O₄ are oxidised.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.2 counts only the oxidation of Fe²⁺ and 0.4 only that of oxalate. 1.67 inverts the electron ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Redox Reactions', balancing of redox reactions
solution.final_answer: Option B: 0.6

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a redox reaction?

solution.concept: Identifying redox reactions by oxidation numbers
solution.explanation: A reaction is a redox reaction if the oxidation number of at least one element changes. In the decomposition of CaCO₃, Ca stays +2, C stays +4 and O stays −2.
steps: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂: no change in any oxidation number → not redox
solution.why_others_wrong: In each of the other three reactions an element changes its oxidation number.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Redox Reactions', redox reactions in terms of oxidation number
solution.final_answer: Option C: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell works with an efficiency of about 70%, much higher than that of a thermal power plant (about 40%).
Reason (R): In a fuel cell, the chemical energy of the fuel is converted directly into electrical energy.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: A thermal power plant first converts chemical energy into heat, then into mechanical and finally electrical energy, losing energy at each step. A fuel cell converts the free energy of the reaction directly into electrical energy, which is why its efficiency is much higher. Both statements are true and R explains A.
steps: Thermal plant: chemical → heat → mechanical → electrical (about 40%)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', fuel cells
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given the standard reduction potentials Ag⁺/Ag = +0.80 V, Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V, Fe²⁺/Fe = −0.44 V and Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Iron displaces silver from an aqueous solution of AgNO₃.
(b) Copper displaces zinc from an aqueous solution of ZnSO₄.
(c) Among the four metals, silver is the weakest reducing agent.
(d) Among the four cations, Ag⁺ is the strongest oxidising agent.
(e) The standard emf of the cell Zn | Zn²⁺ || Fe²⁺ | Fe is 1.20 V.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The higher the reduction potential, the stronger the cation as an oxidising agent and the weaker the metal as a reducing agent. A metal with a lower E° can reduce the cation of a metal with a higher E°.
steps: (a) True: E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) < E°(Ag⁺/Ag) → Fe reduces Ag⁺
(c) True: Ag⁺/Ag has the highest E° → Ag is the weakest reducing agent
(e) False: E° = −0.44 − (−0.76) = +0.32 V; 1.20 V adds the two potentials
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (b) or (e) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', electrochemical series and electrode potential
solution.final_answer: Option A: (a), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, oxygen is oxidised at the anode.
Statement II: Catalysts such as finely divided platinum or palladium are incorporated into the electrodes of the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: In this fuel cell hydrogen is oxidised at the anode and oxygen is reduced at the cathode: O₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻(aq). So Statement I is false. Finely divided Pt or Pd is incorporated into the porous carbon electrodes to increase the rate of the electrode reactions: Statement II is true.
steps: Pt/Pd catalysts in the electrodes (II true)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', fuel cells
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The molar conductivity of a 0.010 M solution of a weak monobasic acid HA is 40 S cm² mol⁻¹, and its limiting molar conductivity is 400 S cm² mol⁻¹. Its dissociation constant, K_a = cα²/(1 − α), is:

solution.concept: Degree of dissociation from molar conductivity
solution.explanation: For a weak electrolyte the degree of dissociation α = Λm/Λ°m. K_a then follows from Ostwald's expression.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ drops the (1 − α) term that the stem asks for. 1.11 × 10⁻³ uses α instead of α². 1.11 × 10⁻² leaves out the concentration c.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', applications of Kohlrausch law: dissociation constant of weak electrolytes
solution.final_answer: Option D: 1.11 × 10⁻⁴

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A conductivity cell filled with KCl solution of conductivity 0.14 S m⁻¹ has a resistance of 150 Ω. The same cell filled with a 0.050 mol L⁻¹ solution of an electrolyte X has a resistance of 420 Ω. The molar conductivity of the solution of X is:

solution.explanation: The KCl solution calibrates the cell: G* = κR. The same cell constant gives the conductivity of X, and Λm = κ/c with c in mol m⁻³ for SI units.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 S m² mol⁻¹ divides by c in mol L⁻¹ without converting to mol m⁻³. 7.84 × 10⁻³ multiplies by the resistance ratio the wrong way round. 5.0 × 10⁻² is the conductivity, not the molar conductivity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', measurement of the conductivity of ionic solutions
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1.0 × 10⁻³ S m² mol⁻¹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (electrode reaction) with List-II (where it takes place).

List-I:
A. Pb(s) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + 2e⁻
B. PbO₂(s) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + 4H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄(s) + 2H₂O(l)
C. Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
D. MnO₂ + NH₄⁺ + e⁻ → MnO(OH) + NH₃

List-II:
I. Cathode of the dry cell
II. Anode of the lead storage battery during discharge
III. Anode of the dry cell
IV. Cathode of the lead storage battery during discharge

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Electrode reactions of the lead storage battery and the dry cell
solution.explanation: Oxidation (loss of electrons) occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode. During discharge of the lead storage battery, lead is oxidised to PbSO₄ and PbO₂ is reduced to PbSO₄. In the dry cell, the zinc container is oxidised and MnO₂ is reduced (Mn: +4 → +3).
steps: Pb → PbSO₄ (oxidation) → lead battery anode → II
PbO₂ → PbSO₄ (reduction) → lead battery cathode → IV
Zn → Zn²⁺ (oxidation) → dry cell anode → III
MnO₂ → MnO(OH) (reduction) → dry cell cathode → I
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap anode and cathode in one of the two cells, or put the zinc oxidation in the lead battery.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', batteries: dry cell and lead storage battery
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At the same concentration and temperature, an aqueous solution of HCl conducts electricity better than an aqueous solution of NaCl.
Reason (R): Pure hydrogen chloride is a gas at room temperature, whereas pure sodium chloride is a solid.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Ionic conductivities of H⁺ and Na⁺
solution.explanation: Both HCl and NaCl are strong electrolytes, so the difference lies in the ions. The limiting molar conductivity of H⁺ (about 350 S cm² mol⁻¹) is about seven times that of Na⁺ (about 50 S cm² mol⁻¹), so the HCl solution conducts better: A is true. R is also true, but the physical state of the pure substances has nothing to do with the conductance of their aqueous solutions, so R does not explain A.
steps: Λ°(H⁺) ≈ 350 vs Λ°(Na⁺) ≈ 50 S cm² mol⁻¹ → HCl(aq) conducts better (A true)
HCl is a gas and NaCl a solid (R true) but irrelevant to conduction in solution
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', Kohlrausch law: limiting molar conductivities of ions
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For a first-order reaction, the percentage of the initial reactant that remains unreacted after three half-lives is:

solution.concept: Successive half-lives of a first-order reaction
solution.explanation: The half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on concentration, so the amount halves in every half-life.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% is after two half-lives. 33.3% divides 100% by three. 87.5% is the percentage that has reacted.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', half-life of a reaction
solution.final_answer: Option D: 12.5%

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The instantaneous rate of the reaction R → P at time t is obtained from the plot of [R] against time as:

options.text: The slope of the straight line joining the starting point and the point at time t
The negative of the slope of the tangent to the curve at time t
The area under the curve up to time t
The intercept of the curve on the concentration axis

solution.explanation: The instantaneous rate is −d[R]/dt, the limit of the average rate as the time interval tends to zero. Graphically it is found by drawing a tangent to the [R]–t curve at time t and taking the negative of its slope.
steps: Draw a tangent at t; rate = −(slope of tangent)
solution.why_others_wrong: The line joining two points gives an average rate. The area under the curve and the intercept have no such meaning.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', rate of a chemical reaction: instantaneous rate
solution.final_answer: Option B: The negative of the slope of the tangent to the curve at time t

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For two reactions with the same pre-exponential factor at the same temperature, the reaction with the higher activation energy has the smaller rate constant.
Statement II: The rate constant of a first-order reaction has the unit mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Arrhenius equation and units of k
solution.explanation: k = A e^(−Ea/RT): with A and T fixed, a larger Ea gives a smaller e^(−Ea/RT) and so a smaller k. Statement I is true. For a first-order reaction k = rate/[R] has the unit s⁻¹; mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ is the unit for a zero-order reaction. Statement II is false.
steps: k = A e^(−Ea/RT): larger Ea → smaller k (I true)
First order: unit of k is s⁻¹ (II false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', temperature dependence of the rate of a reaction; units of rate constant
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A reaction has an activation energy of 28.7 kJ mol⁻¹. At 300 K, the fraction of molecules having energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, e^(−Ea/RT), is (2.303RT = 5.74 kJ mol⁻¹ at 300 K):

solution.concept: Fraction of effective molecules in the Arrhenius equation
solution.explanation: In k = A e^(−Ea/RT), the factor e^(−Ea/RT) is the fraction of molecules with energy at least Ea. Taking logarithms to base 10: log f = −Ea/(2.303RT).
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.7 × 10⁻³ is e⁻⁵: it uses 2.303RT in place of RT inside the natural exponential. 1 × 10⁵ drops the minus sign (a fraction cannot exceed 1). 2 × 10⁻¹ is simply 5.74/28.7.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', temperature dependence of the rate of a reaction
solution.final_answer: Option A: 1 × 10⁻⁵

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The rate constant of a reaction nearly doubles for every 10 K rise in temperature. If this holds, by what factor does the rate constant increase when the temperature is raised from 300 K to 330 K?

solution.concept: Effect of temperature on rate constant
solution.explanation: Each 10 K rise multiplies k by about 2. A 30 K rise contains three such steps, so the factors multiply.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 adds the factors (2 + 2 + 2) instead of multiplying them. 3 counts the steps. 9 is 3².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', temperature dependence of the rate of a reaction
solution.final_answer: Option C: 8

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The thermal decomposition of HI on a gold surface is a zero-order reaction.
Reason (R): Gold is a noble metal that does not corrode in air.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT gives the decomposition of HI on a gold surface as an example of a zero-order reaction, so A is true. Gold is indeed unreactive towards air, so R is true. But R does not explain A: the zero order arises because the gold surface is saturated with HI molecules, so the rate does not depend on the gas concentration.
steps: Reason for zero order: saturated catalyst surface, not resistance to corrosion
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', zero order reactions
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (expression) with List-II (what it represents).

List-I:
A. k = (2.303/t) log([R]₀/[R])
B. [R] = [R]₀ − kt
C. t½ = 0.693/k
D. t½ = [R]₀/2k

List-II:
I. Integrated rate equation of a zero-order reaction
II. Half-life of a first-order reaction
III. Integrated rate equation of a first-order reaction
IV. Half-life of a zero-order reaction

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: For zero order, [R] falls linearly with time and t½ = [R]₀/2k. For first order, k = (2.303/t) log([R]₀/[R]) and t½ = 0.693/k.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange the zero- and first-order equations or their half-lives.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', integrated rate equations
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Two first-order reactions, A → products (t½ = 10 min) and B → products (t½ = 20 min), are started at the same time with equal initial concentrations of A and B. After 40 min, the ratio [A] : [B] is:

solution.explanation: In 40 min A goes through 40/10 = 4 half-lives and B through 40/20 = 2 half-lives.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 is just the ratio of the half-lives. 4 : 1 inverts the ratio. 1 : 16 is the fraction of A left, not the ratio of A to B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', half-life of a reaction
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1 : 4

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about a catalyst are correct?

(a) A catalyst is consumed permanently in the reaction it catalyses.
(b) A catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant of a reversible reaction.
(c) A catalyst increases the rate of the forward reaction only.
(d) A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and the backward reactions by the same amount.
(e) A small amount of a catalyst can catalyse a large amount of reactants.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy and is regenerated at the end of the reaction. The energy barrier falls equally for both directions, so both rates rise by the same factor and the position of equilibrium (K) is unchanged. A small amount of catalyst is enough for a large amount of reactants.
steps: (c) False: both directions are speeded up
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (a) or (c) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', effect of catalyst
solution.final_answer: Option A: (b), (d) and (e) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For a first-order reaction, a plot of log[R] (common logarithm) against time t is a straight line whose slope is:

solution.concept: Graphical form of the first-order rate equation
solution.explanation: The integrated first-order equation ln[R] = ln[R]₀ − kt becomes, in common logarithms, log[R] = log[R]₀ − kt/2.303.
solution.why_others_wrong: −k is the slope of the ln[R] plot, not the log[R] plot. −2.303k multiplies instead of dividing. The slope is negative because [R] falls with time.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', first order reactions
solution.final_answer: Option C: −k/2.303

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text: The Cl–Cl bond distance in the chlorine molecule is 198 pm. The covalent (atomic) radius of chlorine is:

solution.explanation: For a non-metal forming a homonuclear diatomic molecule, the covalent radius is half the distance between the nuclei of the two bonded atoms.
steps: Covalent radius = ½ × internuclear distance = 198 / 2 = 99 pm
solution.why_others_wrong: 198 pm is the whole bond length. 396 pm doubles it, and 49.5 pm halves the radius again.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', atomic radius
solution.final_answer: Option A: 99 pm

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text: An element has the ground-state electronic configuration [Ne] 3s² 3p³. Its position in the periodic table is:

solution.concept: Locating an element from its configuration
solution.explanation: The period is the principal quantum number of the valence shell. For a p-block element, the group number is 10 + (number of s and p valence electrons).
solution.why_others_wrong: Group 13 counts only the s electrons plus one p electron. Period 2 ignores the [Ne] core. Group 5 is a d-block group; the old 'VA' label is now group 15.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', electronic configurations and types of elements: p-block
solution.final_answer: Option D: Period 3, group 15

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The s-block and p-block elements together are called the representative or main group elements.
Statement II: The f-block elements are called the inner-transition elements.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Types of elements in the periodic table
solution.explanation: Both statements are the standard classification: s- and p-block elements are the representative (main group) elements, d-block elements are the transition elements, and the lanthanoids and actinoids (f-block) are the inner-transition elements.
steps: s + p blocks → representative elements (I true)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', electronic configurations and types of elements
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs of elements shows a diagonal relationship?

solution.explanation: The first member of groups 1 and 2 (Li, Be) resembles the second member of the next group (Mg, Al) more than its own group. This similarity between diagonally placed elements is called a diagonal relationship.
solution.why_others_wrong: Be–Mg, Li–Na and B–Al are pairs in the same group, not diagonal pairs.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', anomalous properties of second period elements
solution.final_answer: Option B: Beryllium and aluminium

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Among the elements of the second period, neon has the lowest first ionisation enthalpy.
Reason (R): Neon has a completely filled valence shell, 2s² 2p⁶.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: A completely filled valence shell is very stable, and neon also has the highest effective nuclear charge in the period. Its first ionisation enthalpy is therefore the highest, not the lowest, in period 2 (lithium has the lowest). A is false; R is true.
steps: Closed shell + high Z_eff → highest ΔiH₁ in period 2 (A false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', ionisation enthalpy
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (general outer electronic configuration) with List-II (group).

List-I:
A. [noble gas] ns² np⁶
B. [noble gas] (n−1)d¹⁰ ns²
C. [noble gas] ns¹
D. [noble gas] (n−1)d⁵ ns¹

List-II:
I. Group 6
II. Group 1
III. Group 18
IV. Group 12

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Group from the outer electronic configuration
solution.explanation: For s-block elements the group equals the number of s electrons; for p-block, 10 + (s + p electrons); for d-block, the number of (n−1)d + ns electrons.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap group 1 with group 6, or group 18 with group 12.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', electronic configurations and types of elements
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Which of the following general formulae (M = metal, E = element of the group) are correct?

(a) Oxide of a group 2 element: MO
(b) Simple hydride of a group 14 element: EH₄
(c) Simple hydride of a group 16 element: EH₃
(d) Simple hydride of a group 15 element: EH₂
(e) Oxide of a group 13 element in its group oxidation state: E₂O₃

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The usual valence of a representative element equals the number of valence electrons (groups 1, 2, 13, 14) or 8 minus that number (groups 15–17). Group 2: valence 2 → MO. Group 14: valence 4 → EH₄ (CH₄). Group 16: valence 2 → H₂E (H₂O). Group 15: valence 3 → EH₃ (NH₃). Group 13: valence 3 → E₂O₃ (Al₂O₃).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (c) or (d) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', periodic trends in valence
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (e) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text: The element with atomic number 114 is placed in the periodic table in:

solution.concept: Predicting the position of a heavy element
solution.explanation: The seventh period begins at Z = 87 and ends at Z = 118 (group 18). Element 114 is four places before 118, so it is in group 18 − 4 = 14, in the p-block of period 7, below lead.
solution.why_others_wrong: Group 16 would be Z = 116. Period 6 ends at Z = 86. Group 4 of period 7 is Z = 104.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', nomenclature of elements with atomic numbers > 100; long form of periodic table
solution.final_answer: Option A: Period 7, group 14 (p-block)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The listed atomic radii of the noble gases are larger than those of the halogens of the same periods.
Reason (R): For the noble gases van der Waals (non-bonded) radii are quoted, whereas for the halogens covalent radii are quoted, and van der Waals radii are larger.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Noble gases are monatomic and do not form ordinary covalent bonds, so only their van der Waals radii can be measured. A van der Waals radius (half the distance between non-bonded neighbours) is much larger than a covalent radius. This is why the noble gases appear to break the trend of decreasing radius across a period. R explains A.
steps: Noble gases: van der Waals radii
Apparent increase at group 18 is due to the different definition
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', atomic radius (noble gases)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Chemical reactivity tends to be high for the elements at the two extremes of a period and lower for the elements in the middle.
Statement II: The high reactivity of the group 1 metals is due to their high ionisation enthalpies.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: On the left of a period the metals lose electrons readily, and on the right the non-metals gain electrons readily, so reactivity is highest at the two ends: Statement I is true. Alkali metals are reactive because their ionisation enthalpies are low, which makes electron loss easy; Statement II is false.
steps: Left end: easy electron loss (low ΔiH); right end: easy electron gain (very negative ΔegH) (I true)
Group 1 reactivity comes from low, not high, ionisation enthalpy (II false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', periodic trends in chemical properties: reactivity
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Among the hydrides NH₃, PH₃, AsH₃ and SbH₃, the one with the lowest boiling point is:

solution.explanation: From PH₃ to SbH₃ the boiling point rises with molecular size because van der Waals forces increase. NH₃ has an abnormally high boiling point because its molecules are hydrogen bonded. So PH₃ has the lowest boiling point (about 185 K, against about 238 K for NH₃).
steps: PH₃ < AsH₃ < SbH₃: larger molecules, stronger van der Waals forces
NH₃ is raised above PH₃ by hydrogen bonding
solution.why_others_wrong: NH₃ is hydrogen bonded, and AsH₃ and SbH₃ are larger molecules with stronger dispersion forces, so all three boil above PH₃.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 15 elements: properties of hydrides
solution.final_answer: Option B: PH₃

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (group 16 element) with List-II (its nature).

List-I:
A. Oxygen
B. Sulphur
C. Tellurium
D. Polonium

List-II:
I. Metal
II. Metalloid
III. Non-metal, solid at room temperature
IV. Non-metal, gas at room temperature

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Metallic character increases down group 16: oxygen and sulphur are non-metals (oxygen a gas, sulphur a solid), selenium and tellurium are metalloids and polonium is a metal.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange oxygen and sulphur, or tellurium and polonium, or sulphur and tellurium.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 16 elements: physical properties
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Helium has the lowest boiling point of any known substance.
Statement II: The first ionisation enthalpy of the noble gases increases down the group.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Physical properties of the noble gases
solution.explanation: Helium boils at about 4.2 K, the lowest boiling point of any substance, because only very weak dispersion forces act between its tiny atoms: Statement I is true. Down group 18 the atomic size increases, so the ionisation enthalpy decreases: Statement II is false.
steps: He: b.p. ≈ 4.2 K, the lowest known (I true)
Size increases down the group → ΔiH decreases (II false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 18 elements: physical properties and ionisation enthalpy
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The first member of each group of the p-block differs from the other members of its group. Which of the following is NOT a reason for this anomalous behaviour?

options.text: Availability of d orbitals in its valence shell

solution.concept: Reasons for the anomalous behaviour of the first member
solution.explanation: The first member of each p-block group is anomalous because of its small size, high electronegativity, high ionisation enthalpy and the ABSENCE of d orbitals in its valence shell (n = 2 has only s and p orbitals).
steps: Second-period valence shell: 2s and 2p only → no d orbitals
Small size, high electronegativity and high ionisation enthalpy are genuine reasons
solution.why_others_wrong: Small size, high electronegativity and high ionisation enthalpy are all listed causes of the anomaly; it is the lack, not the presence, of d orbitals that matters.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', anomalous behaviour of the first member of p-block groups
solution.final_answer: Option D: Availability of d orbitals in its valence shell

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which element of group 13 has the highest electronegativity (Pauling scale)?

solution.explanation: Boron, the small first member, has the highest electronegativity in the group (about 2.0). Down the group electronegativity first falls from B to Al (1.5) and then rises slightly (Ga 1.6, In 1.7, Tl 1.8) because of differences in atomic size, but none of the heavier members reaches boron's value.
solution.why_others_wrong: The slight rise from Al to Tl misleads some students into choosing Tl or Ga; aluminium has the lowest value in the group.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', group 13 elements: electronegativity
solution.final_answer: Option C: Boron

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The heavier elements of groups 15 and 16 can form dπ–pπ bonds, but nitrogen and oxygen cannot.
Reason (R): Nitrogen and oxygen have no d orbitals in their valence shells.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: dπ–pπ bonding and the first element
solution.explanation: Phosphorus and the heavier elements have vacant d orbitals in their valence shells, which they can use to form dπ–pπ bonds (for example with oxygen). Nitrogen and oxygen, in the second period, have only 2s and 2p orbitals, so they cannot form such bonds; they form pπ–pπ multiple bonds instead. R explains A.
steps: Heavier elements: vacant d orbitals → dπ–pπ bonding possible
N, O: no valence d orbitals (R) → no dπ–pπ bonding (A)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 15: anomalous properties of nitrogen
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Down group 15, the covalent radius increases considerably from nitrogen to phosphorus but only slightly from arsenic to bismuth.
Statement II: The small increase from arsenic to bismuth is due to the presence of completely filled d and/or f orbitals in the heavier members, which shield the nucleus poorly.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Both statements describe the NCERT trend. A new shell causes a large jump from N to P. In As, Sb and Bi the extra nuclear charge is poorly shielded by filled d (and in Bi also f) orbitals, so the radius increases only slightly.
steps: As → Bi: small increase due to poor shielding by d/f electrons (II true)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 15 elements: atomic and ionic radii
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (group) with List-II (trend in oxidation state down the group, due to the inert pair effect).

List-I:
A. Group 13
B. Group 14
C. Group 15
D. Group 16

List-II:
I. +3 becomes more stable than +5
II. +1 becomes more stable than +3
III. +4 becomes more stable than +6
IV. +2 becomes more stable than +4

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Down groups 13 to 16 the ns² electrons become increasingly reluctant to take part in bonding, so an oxidation state two less than the group oxidation state becomes more stable for the heavier members.
steps: Group 13 (ns² np¹): +1 more stable than +3 down the group (e.g. Tl) → II
Group 14 (ns² np²): +2 more stable than +4 (e.g. Pb) → IV
Group 15 (ns² np³): +3 more stable than +5 (e.g. Bi) → I
Group 16 (ns² np⁴): +4 more stable than +6 → III
solution.why_others_wrong: Each group's lower stable state is the group oxidation state minus two; the other codes break this pattern.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', oxidation states of groups 15 and 16; Class 11 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', groups 13 and 14
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the group 17 elements are correct?

(a) They have the smallest atomic radii in their respective periods.
(b) The bond dissociation enthalpy of I₂ is higher than that of Br₂.
(c) They have very high ionisation enthalpies, so they have little tendency to lose electrons.
(d) Their melting and boiling points increase steadily from fluorine to iodine.
(e) Iodine is more electronegative than chlorine.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Halogens have the highest effective nuclear charge in their periods, hence the smallest radii and very high ionisation enthalpies. Their melting and boiling points rise with molecular size from F₂ to I₂. The bond dissociation enthalpy decreases from Cl₂ to I₂ (Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂) as the atoms get larger, and electronegativity decreases down the group.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (b) or (e) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 17 elements: atomic and physical properties
solution.final_answer: Option A: (a), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following correctly describes the tendency of the group 14 elements to show catenation?

options.text: All five elements catenate strongly, in the order C > Si > Ge > Sn > Pb
Sn > Ge > Si > C; lead catenates the most
C ≫ Si > Ge ≈ Sn; lead does not show catenation

solution.explanation: Catenation depends on the strength of the E–E bond. The C–C bond is strong, so carbon catenates far more than any other element. E–E bond strength falls down the group, giving C ≫ Si > Ge ≈ Sn, and lead does not show catenation.
solution.why_others_wrong: Silicon catenates much less than carbon. Lead does not catenate, so orders that include strong catenation by Pb, or that reverse the trend, are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', group 14 elements: anomalous behaviour of carbon (catenation)
solution.final_answer: Option D: C ≫ Si > Ge ≈ Sn; lead does not show catenation

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The tendency of the group 15 elements to show the −3 oxidation state decreases down the group.
Reason (R): The electronegativity of the elements increases down group 15.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Down group 15 the atoms get larger and more metallic, so the tendency to gain three electrons (−3 state) decreases; bismuth hardly forms any compound in the −3 state. A is true. Electronegativity decreases, not increases, down the group, so R is false.
steps: Size and metallic character increase down the group → −3 tendency decreases (A true)
Electronegativity: N > P > As > Sb > Bi (R false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 15 elements: oxidation states
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The colour of the halogens becomes lighter from F₂ to I₂.
Statement II: The halogens are coloured because their molecules absorb radiation in the visible region, which excites their outer electrons to higher energy levels.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: The halogens are coloured because absorption of visible light excites their outer electrons; the colour seen is the complementary colour. As the molecules get larger, less energy is needed for the excitation, so the colour deepens from pale yellow F₂ to violet I₂. Statement I is false; Statement II is true.
steps: Absorption of visible light → electronic excitation → colour (II true)
Smaller excitation energy down the group → colour deepens, not lightens (I false)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 17 elements: physical properties
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the group 16 elements are correct?

(a) The first ionisation enthalpy increases down the group.
(b) The melting and boiling points increase down the group up to tellurium.
(c) The large difference between the melting and boiling points of oxygen and sulphur arises because oxygen exists as diatomic O₂ molecules whereas sulphur exists as polyatomic S₈ molecules.
(d) The atomic radius decreases from oxygen to tellurium.
(e) The electronegativity decreases from oxygen to polonium.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Down the group the size increases, so ionisation enthalpy and electronegativity decrease. Melting and boiling points rise from O to Te with increasing size and atomicity; oxygen (O₂) has much weaker van der Waals forces than sulphur (S₈).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (a) or (d) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The p-Block Elements', group 16 elements: atomic and physical properties
solution.final_answer: Option B: (b), (c) and (e) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Leaving out palladium, which is an exception, the general outer electronic configuration of the d-block elements is:

solution.concept: Electronic configuration of the d-block elements
solution.explanation: In the d-block, the (n−1)d orbitals are being filled while the outermost ns orbital holds one or two electrons. Palladium (4d¹⁰ 5s⁰) is the exception NCERT mentions.
steps: d-block: inner (n−1)d subshell filled progressively, d¹ to d¹⁰
Outer ns subshell: 1 or 2 electrons (e.g. Cr 3d⁵ 4s¹, Fe 3d⁶ 4s²)
solution.why_others_wrong: ns² np¹⁻⁶ is the p-block configuration. (n−2)f¹⁻¹⁴ (n−1)d⁰⁻¹ ns² is the f-block (inner transition) configuration. (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰ fits only palladium, the stated exception.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', electronic configurations of the d-block elements
solution.final_answer: Option B: (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻²

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The spin-only magnetic moment of the V³⁺ ion (Z of V = 23) is about:

solution.explanation: V is [Ar] 3d³ 4s². Removing the two 4s electrons and one 3d electron leaves V³⁺ = [Ar] 3d², with two unpaired electrons.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.73 BM is for one unpaired electron. 3.87 BM is for three (V²⁺, 3d³). 4.90 BM is for four unpaired electrons.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', magnetic properties (spin-only formula)
solution.final_answer: Option C: 2.83 BM

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Samarium (Z = 62) has the configuration [Xe] 4f⁶ 6s². The number of 4f electrons in the Sm³⁺ ion is:

solution.explanation: To form Ln³⁺, the two 6s electrons are lost first and then one 4f electron (there is no 5d electron in Sm).
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 is the 4f count of the neutral atom (or of Sm²⁺). 3 confuses the charge with the 4f count. 8 is Z − 54 without removing any electrons.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', the lanthanoids (electronic configurations)
solution.final_answer: Option A: 5

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The electronic configuration of lanthanum (Z = 57) is [Xe] 4f¹ 6s².
Statement II: Yb²⁺, which has a 4f¹⁴ configuration, acts as a reducing agent.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Configurations and oxidation states of the lanthanoids
solution.explanation: Lanthanum is [Xe] 5d¹ 6s²; its 4f subshell is empty. NCERT notes that Yb²⁺ (f¹⁴), like Eu²⁺, is a reductant, changing to the common +3 state.
steps: Statement II: Yb²⁺ (4f¹⁴) is oxidised to Yb³⁺, so it is a reducing agent → true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', the lanthanoids (electronic configurations, oxidation states)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 25.0 mL of 0.10 M sodium sulphite solution is oxidised to sulphate by acidified 0.020 M KMnO₄ solution (permanganate is reduced to Mn²⁺). The volume of KMnO₄ solution needed is:

solution.explanation: MnO₄⁻ gains 5 electrons (Mn +7 → +2) and SO₃²⁻ loses 2 electrons (S +4 → +6), so 2 MnO₄⁻ react with 5 SO₃²⁻: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5SO₃²⁻ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5SO₄²⁻ + 3H₂O.
solution.shortcut: Equivalents: 2.5 × 2 = 5 meq of sulphite = 0.020 × 5 × V → V = 50 mL.
solution.why_others_wrong: 125 mL takes a 1 : 1 mole ratio. 83.3 mL treats permanganate as gaining 3 electrons (reduction to MnO₂, which happens only in neutral solution). 312.5 mL inverts the 2 : 5 ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', potassium permanganate (oxidising action in acid solution)
solution.final_answer: Option B: 50 mL

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The second ionisation enthalpies of chromium and copper are unusually high compared with those of their neighbours in the 3d series.
Reason (R): Removing the second electron from Cr⁺ (3d⁵) or Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) breaks up a stable half-filled or completely filled d subshell.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Irregularities in the ionisation enthalpies of the 3d series
solution.explanation: After the first ionisation, Cr⁺ is 3d⁵ and Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰. NCERT points out that the second ionisation enthalpies are higher for Cr and Cu precisely because these M⁺ ions have the stable d⁵ and d¹⁰ configurations, which must be disturbed.
steps: The second electron must come from the stable d⁵ / d¹⁰ set → high IE₂ (A true)
R states exactly this cause → R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', ionisation enthalpies
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the species in List-I with its ground-state electronic configuration in List-II (atomic numbers: Cr 24, Fe 26, Co 27, Zn 30).

List-I:
A. Cr
B. Zn²⁺
C. Fe³⁺
D. Co³⁺

List-II:
I. [Ar] 3d⁶
II. [Ar] 3d⁵
III. [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹
IV. [Ar] 3d¹⁰

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Chromium takes the half-filled 3d⁵ 4s¹ arrangement. Ions of the 3d metals lose their 4s electrons first.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-II, C-III gives Fe³⁺ a 4s electron, but 4s electrons are lost first. C-I, D-II swaps the d counts of Fe³⁺ and Co³⁺. B-II, C-IV mixes up Zn²⁺ and Fe³⁺.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', electronic configurations
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the metals of the 3d series are correct?

(a) The atomic radii decrease at first along the series and then change very little for the middle elements.
(b) The density of the metals generally increases from titanium to copper.
(c) Zinc has the highest enthalpy of atomisation in the series.
(d) Metals with very high enthalpies of atomisation tend to be noble in their reactions.
(e) Ti⁴⁺ compounds are coloured because Ti⁴⁺ has unpaired 3d electrons.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Radii fall at first and then level off in the middle (Fe, Co, Ni are almost the same size), so density rises from Ti to Cu as mass increases. Zinc, with no unpaired d electrons, has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation. Ti⁴⁺ is 3d⁰, so its compounds are colourless (white TiO₂).
steps: (a) radii decrease, then nearly constant → true
(c) Zn has the lowest, not highest, enthalpy of atomisation → false
(d) high atomisation enthalpy → noble behaviour (NCERT) → true
(e) Ti⁴⁺ is d⁰, no unpaired electrons → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Each other option includes (c) or (e), which are false, or leaves out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', physical properties, atomic sizes, enthalpies of atomisation
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The actinoids show a greater range of oxidation states than the lanthanoids. This is attributed mainly to the fact that:

options.text: the 5f orbitals are buried more deeply in the atom than the 4f orbitals
the 5f, 6d and 7s levels are of comparable energies
the actinoid contraction is smaller than the lanthanoid contraction

solution.explanation: Because the 5f, 6d and 7s levels lie close in energy, a variable number of electrons can be used in bonding, so the actinoids show many oxidation states.
steps: Range of oxidation states depends on how many electrons can be removed at similar cost
5f, 6d and 7s are of comparable energies → variable oxidation states
solution.why_others_wrong: The 5f orbitals are less deeply buried than 4f, not more, so the first option is reversed. Radioactivity does not decide oxidation states. The actinoid contraction is in fact greater from element to element, and in any case contraction does not explain the range.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', the actinoids (oxidation states)
solution.final_answer: Option B: the 5f, 6d and 7s levels are of comparable energies

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In neutral solution, in the presence of zinc sulphate, permanganate oxidises Mn²⁺ ions to MnO₂ and is itself reduced to MnO₂. When 0.020 mol of MnO₄⁻ reacts completely with Mn²⁺ in this way, the total mass of MnO₂ formed is (Mn = 55, O = 16):

solution.explanation: MnO₄⁻ (+7) gains 3 electrons and Mn²⁺ loses 2 electrons, both ending at +4. Balancing electrons: 2MnO₄⁻ + 3Mn²⁺ + 2H₂O → 5MnO₂ + 4H⁺. Both reactants end up as MnO₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.74 g counts only the MnO₂ coming from permanganate, and 2.61 g only that from Mn²⁺. 3.48 g assumes a 1 : 1 ratio of MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', potassium permanganate (oxidising action in neutral solution)
solution.final_answer: Option D: 4.35 g

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about potassium permanganate and potassium dichromate are correct?

(a) In neutral or faintly alkaline solution, each MnO₄⁻ ion gains three electrons.
(b) In acidic solution, each Cr₂O₇²⁻ ion gains six electrons.
(c) The manganate and permanganate ions are both tetrahedral.
(d) Commercially, manganate is converted into permanganate by electrolytic oxidation in alkaline solution.
(e) In acidic solution, one MnO₄⁻ ion oxidises three Fe²⁺ ions.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Structures and electron changes of permanganate and dichromate
solution.explanation: MnO₄⁻ → MnO₂ in neutral/faintly alkaline solution is +7 → +4 (3e⁻). Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ is 2 × 3 = 6e⁻. Both MnO₄²⁻ and MnO₄⁻ are tetrahedral. Industrially, MnO₂ is fused with alkali and an oxidant to give manganate, which is then oxidised electrolytically to permanganate in alkaline solution. In acid, MnO₄⁻ gains 5e⁻ and so oxidises five Fe²⁺ ions.
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option containing (e) is wrong; (a), (c), (d) only leaves out the true statement (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate
solution.final_answer: Option A: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): MnO is a basic oxide, whereas Mn₂O₇ is an acidic oxide.
Reason (R): As the oxidation state of a metal increases, the ionic character of its oxides decreases and their acidic character increases.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Nature of the oxides of transition metals
solution.explanation: In MnO, manganese is +2 and the oxide is ionic and basic. In Mn₂O₇ (+7, a covalent green oil) the oxide is acidic, giving permanganic acid. NCERT relates this to the fall in ionic character with rising oxidation state.
steps: Higher oxidation state → less ionic, more acidic oxide (R true and explains A)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', oxides and oxoanions of metals
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Applying Hund's rule to the free (gaseous) ions, how many of the following have the same number of unpaired electrons, and hence the same spin-only magnetic moment, as Fe²⁺?
Ti²⁺, Cr²⁺, Mn³⁺, Fe³⁺, Co³⁺, Ni²⁺
(Atomic numbers: Ti 22, Cr 24, Mn 25, Fe 26, Co 27, Ni 28)

solution.concept: Unpaired electrons from the d-electron count
solution.explanation: Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ with four unpaired electrons. A d⁴ ion (four singly occupied orbitals) and another d⁶ ion also have four unpaired electrons.
steps: Same as Fe²⁺: Cr²⁺, Mn³⁺, Co³⁺ → 3
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 misses Co³⁺, which is isoelectronic with Fe²⁺. 4 wrongly adds Fe³⁺ (five unpaired). 5 also adds both d² and d⁸ ions, which have only two unpaired electrons.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', magnetic properties
solution.final_answer: Option B: 3

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The IUPAC name of [Cr(NH₃)₃(H₂O)₃]Cl₃ is:

solution.explanation: Ligands are named in alphabetical order (ammine before aqua; the prefix tri is ignored). The complex is a cation, so the metal keeps its ordinary name, followed by its oxidation state.
solution.why_others_wrong: Triaquatriammine breaks the alphabetical order. 'Chromate' is used only for an anionic complex. (II) gives the wrong oxidation state.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', nomenclature of coordination compounds
solution.final_answer: Option C: Triamminetriaquachromium(III) chloride

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the coordination entity in List-I with the oxidation state of its central metal in List-II.

List-I:
A. [Ni(CO)₄]
B. [Ag(CN)₂]⁻
C. [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺
D. [PtCl₆]²⁻

List-II:
I. +2
II. 0
III. +4
IV. +1

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Oxidation number of the central atom
solution.explanation: Oxidation number = charge on the entity − total charge of the ligands. CO and NH₃ are neutral; CN⁻ and Cl⁻ carry −1 each.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, B-II swaps nickel and silver. B-I, C-IV gives silver +2 and copper +1. C-III, D-I gives copper +4 and platinum +2, ignoring the six chloride ligands.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', definitions (oxidation number of central atom)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The formula of tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate is:

solution.concept: Writing a formula from the name
solution.explanation: The name gives a complex cation with four ammine ligands and Cu(II), so the cation is [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺. One sulphate ion (2−) balances it.
solution.why_others_wrong: (SO₄)₂ would need copper(IV). [Cu(SO₄)(NH₃)₄] puts sulphate inside the coordination sphere, which the name (no 'sulphato') does not say. [Cu(NH₃)₂]SO₄ has only two ammine ligands.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', formulas of mononuclear coordination entities
solution.final_answer: Option D: [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Optical isomers (enantiomers) are mirror images of each other that cannot be superimposed on one another.
Statement II: Optical isomerism is common in octahedral complexes containing didentate ligands.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT defines optical isomers as non-superimposable mirror images and notes that optical isomerism is common in octahedral complexes involving didentate ligands, such as [Co(en)₃]³⁺.
steps: Statement I: definition of enantiomers → true
Statement II: e.g. [Co(en)₃]³⁺ and cis-[PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ are chiral → true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', isomerism (optical isomerism)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
